problems.title: A Chance Node Is Just an Average
problems.blurb: No adversary, no worst case -- a chance node's value is the plain mean of its children.
problems.statement:
Minimax has two kinds of node: MAX picks the largest child, MIN picks the smallest. Expectimax replaces the adversarial MIN with a CHANCE node -- one that models an opponent (or an environment) that doesn't pick against you, it just acts unpredictably. A CHANCE node's value is the average of its children's values, since with no other information, every outcome is treated as equally likely.

Write chance_value(node): the average value of node's children. You may assume node always has at least one child.
hints: Collect every child's value -- node.children[i].value for a leaf child -- into a list, or just sum them as you go.
The average of n numbers is their sum divided by n. Use len(node.children) for n.
return sum(c.value for c in node.children) / len(node.children).

tests.name: evenly split values
tests.src: assert chance_value(build([1, 2])) == 1.5

tests.name: all children equal
tests.src: assert chance_value(build([3, 3, 3])) == 3.0

tests.name: the example tree
tests.src:
got = chance_value(build([10, 4, 20, 6]))
assert got == 10.0, got

tests.name: random flat trees, checked against a direct average
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(31)
for _ in range(200):
    values = [random.randint(-20, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    got = chance_value(build(values))
    want = sum(values) / len(values)
    assert abs(got - want) < 1e-9, (values, got, want)

problems.title: MAX Against an Unpredictable Opponent
problems.blurb: minimax_value with one word changed: CHANCE nodes average instead of minimizing.
problems.statement:
Write expectimax(node, maximizing): the same alternating structure as minimax from the first gym, but the non-MAX levels are CHANCE nodes, not MIN nodes. When maximizing is True, node is a MAX node and its children are CHANCE nodes; when False, node is a CHANCE node (its own value ignored here, same as MIN's structure) and its children are MAX nodes.

MAX
├── [0] CHANCE
│   ├── [0] 8
│   └── [1] 4
└── [1] CHANCE
    ├── [0] 2
    └── [1] 14

The two CHANCE nodes here average to 6.0 and 8.0. MAX then picks the larger: 8.0. Compare that to what plain minimax would compute on the identical tree -- minimax's MIN would pick 4 at the left and 2 at the right, giving MAX only 4 to choose from. Averaging instead of taking the worst case is what makes expectimax less pessimistic than minimax against an opponent who isn't actually your adversary.
problems.examples:
>>> expectimax(build([[8, 4], [2, 14]]), True)
8.0
>>> expectimax(build(5), True)
5
>>> expectimax(build(5), False)
5
hints: Base case: a leaf returns node.value, exactly as in minimax.
Recurse on every child with expectimax(child, not maximizing), same flip as minimax.
If maximizing, return max(...) of those results, same as minimax. If not, return their average instead of min(...) -- sum(values) / len(values).

tests.name: a leaf is its own value either way
tests.src:
assert expectimax(build(5), True) == 5
assert expectimax(build(5), False) == 5

tests.name: the worked example, both directions
tests.src:
tree = build([[8, 4], [2, 14]])
assert expectimax(tree, True) == 8.0, expectimax(tree, True)
assert expectimax(tree, False) == 11.0, expectimax(tree, False)

tests.name: differs from plain minimax on the same tree
tests.src:
tree = build([[8, 4], [2, 14]])
got = expectimax(tree, True)
if got == 4:
    raise AssertionError(
        "4 is what plain minimax gives here (MIN takes the worst case) -- "
        "a CHANCE node should average, not minimize")
assert got == 8.0, got

problems.title: When the Outcomes Aren't Equally Likely
problems.blurb: A chance node's value is a weighted average -- probability times value, summed.
problems.statement:
Real chance nodes rarely have uniform odds -- a loaded die, a weather forecast, an opponent who favors one move. This problem uses a different node type, WNode, where a CHANCE node's children each carry an explicit probability:

wbuild(7)                                    a leaf holding 7
wbuild(("max", [3, 8]))                      a MAX node over two leaves
wbuild(("chance", [(0.25, 2), (0.75, 10)]))  a CHANCE node: 2 with
                                              probability 0.25, 10 with
                                              probability 0.75

Write weighted_expectimax(node). node.kind is either "max" or "chance"; a MAX node's children is a plain list of child nodes, while a CHANCE node's children is a list of (probability, child) pairs whose probabilities sum to 1.

A CHANCE node's value is ∑ probability × value over its children -- not a plain average, since each outcome now counts in proportion to how likely it is.
hints: Base case: node.is_leaf() -- return node.value.
If node.kind == 'max': recurse on each plain child in node.children and return the max of the results.

If node.kind == 'chance': node.children is a list of (prob, child) pairs. For each pair, recurse into weighted_expectimax(child) to get that outcome's value, multiply by prob, and sum all of those products.

tests.name: a leaf is its own value
tests.src: assert weighted_expectimax(wbuild(7)) == 7

tests.name: an uneven chance node
tests.src:
got = weighted_expectimax(wbuild(("chance", [(0.25, 2), (0.75, 10)])))
assert got == 8.0, got

tests.name: a max node over plain leaves
tests.src: assert weighted_expectimax(wbuild(("max", [3, 8]))) == 8

tests.name: the worked example: max over two uneven chance nodes
tests.src:
tree = wbuild(("max", [
    ("chance", [(0.5, 0), (0.5, 20)]),
    ("chance", [(0.9, 5), (0.1, 6)])]))
got = weighted_expectimax(tree)
assert got == 10.0, got

tests.name: using a plain average instead of weighting gives the wrong answer here
tests.src:
tree = wbuild(("chance", [(0.1, 0), (0.9, 100)]))
got = weighted_expectimax(tree)
if got == 50.0:
    raise AssertionError(
        "50.0 is the unweighted average -- multiply each outcome by its "
        "own probability before summing")
assert got == 90.0, got

problems.title: Expectimax With a Depth Limit
problems.blurb: minimax_decision's exact shape, with CHANCE swapped in for MIN -- and no move to report at a chance node.
problems.statement:
Write expectimax_decision(node, limit) for MAX at the root, returning (move, value, leaves) -- the same triple minimax_decision returned in the first gym, and the same shape get_best_move will need on real games.

Every node at depth limit, and every real leaf reached sooner, is evaluated directly and counts as one leaf -- which means every node in the tree needs a value, not just the true leaves at the bottom. That's why the example tree below carries a heuristic estimate at every level, written (h, [children]), the same convention minimax_decision used: without one, a depth cut- off would have nothing meaningful to return.

Levels alternate MAX and CHANCE the same way they alternated MAX and MIN before. The one real difference: a CHANCE node has no "best" child to report -- it doesn't choose, it averages over everything -- so its own move is always None. Only moves chosen at MAX nodes ever matter, and only the very top one is returned. Notice how the chosen move itself, not just the value, changes between limit 1 and limit 2 below -- seeing one more level of the chance node's real spread is enough to flip which branch looks best.
hints: Two helpers, max_value(subtree, depth) and chance_value(subtree, depth), each returning (value, move, leaves). Stop when depth == 0 or subtree.is_leaf(): return (subtree.value, None, 1).

max_value loops over enumerate(subtree.children), recurses into chance_value(child, depth - 1), sums leaves, and keeps the child's index as move only on a strictly better value -- same as minimax_decision.
chance_value has no move to track: sum up every max_value(child, depth - 1)'s value, divide by the number of children, and return (average, None, total_leaves).

tests.name: returns a (move, value, leaves) tuple
tests.src:
got = expectimax_decision(build([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), 2)
assert isinstance(got, tuple) and len(got) == 3, got

tests.name: the worked example at both limits
tests.src:
tree = build((13, [(8, [(12, [(9, []), (15, [])]), (18, [(6, []), (16, [])])]), (9, [(3, [(19, []), (8, [])]), (9, [(3, []), (2, [])])])]))
assert expectimax_decision(tree, 1) == (1, 9, 2), expectimax_decision(tree, 1)
assert expectimax_decision(tree, 2) == (0, 15.0, 4), expectimax_decision(tree, 2)
assert expectimax_decision(tree, 3) == (0, 15.5, 8), expectimax_decision(tree, 3)

tests.name: a chance node never reports a move of its own
tests.src:
# a lopsided tree where the wrong move would look plausible if the chance
# level were mistakenly treated as a decision point
tree = build([[0, 0, 100], [1, 1, 1]])
move, value, leaves = expectimax_decision(tree, 2)
assert move in (0, 1), (move, value, leaves)

problems.title: Counting Every Node, Not Just the Leaves
problems.blurb: The homework's leaf count only tells half the story -- interior nodes cost real work too.
problems.statement:
The first gym's leaf count measures how many terminal positions alpha-beta evaluates. It says nothing about the interior nodes visited along the way -- and on a real search tree, every one of those costs a function call too.

Write alphabeta_visits(node): run alpha-beta for MAX at the root exactly as in figure 5.7, and return (value, total_visits), where total_visits counts every node the search touches -- the root itself, every interior node it recurses into, and every leaf it evaluates. A single leaf counts 1. Figure 5.2's root counts 1 for itself, its 3 MIN children count 1 each, and the 7 leaves alpha-beta actually reads (of the 9 total) bring the count to 11.
hints: Write max_value(subtree, alpha, beta) and min_value(subtree, alpha, beta), each returning (value, visits). A leaf returns (subtree.value, 1) -- it visits only itself.

An interior node visits itself (1) plus every child it recurses into before any cutoff -- start visits = 1, and add each child's visits as you go, even the child that ultimately triggers the cutoff (that child was still visited before the cutoff fired).
The cutoff logic itself (updating alpha/beta, checking value >= beta or value <= alpha) is unchanged from ordinary alpha-beta -- only the bookkeeping you're returning is different.

tests.name: a lone leaf visits only itself
tests.src: assert alphabeta_visits(build(4)) == (4, 1)

tests.name: figure 5.2: root, 3 MIN children, 7 of 9 leaves
tests.src:
got = alphabeta_visits(build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]]))
assert got == (3, 11), got

tests.name: leaves alone undercounts -- interior nodes must be included too
tests.src:
got = alphabeta_visits(build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]]))
if got == (3, 7):
    raise AssertionError(
        "(3, 7) is the leaf-only count -- add 1 for every interior node "
        "visited too, including the root")

problems.title: How Many Times Did Pruning Actually Fire?
problems.blurb: Not every early return is a cutoff -- the last child in a loop always 'returns early' too, without anything being pruned.
problems.statement:
Write alphabeta_cutoffs(node): run alpha-beta for MAX at the root, and return (value, cutoffs), where cutoffs counts how many times the pruning condition (value >= beta at a MAX node, value <= alpha at a MIN node) actually fired and skipped remaining children.

Be careful what counts. A node that finishes its loop normally, having looked at every child, is not a cutoff -- even though its function call is about to return, nothing was skipped. Only count a node once, the moment its cutoff condition trips and it stops early, abandoning children it would otherwise have explored.
hints: Same max_value/min_value shape as ordinary alpha-beta, each returning (value, cutoffs) instead of just (value, leaves).
Accumulate the cutoff counts your children report, the same way you'd accumulate a leaf count -- cutoffs += child_cutoffs inside the loop.

The moment your own cutoff condition trips, add exactly 1 more (for this node's own cutoff) before returning -- return value, cutoffs + 1. If the loop finishes without ever tripping, return cutoffs unchanged, with no +1.

tests.name: a lone leaf has no cutoffs at all
tests.src: assert alphabeta_cutoffs(build(4)) == (4, 0)

tests.name: a tree with no pruning: every value improves the bound but never trips it
tests.src:
got = alphabeta_cutoffs(build([[1, 2], [3, 4]]))
assert got == (3, 0), got

tests.name: figure 5.2: exactly two cutoffs, at the second and third MIN nodes
tests.src:
got = alphabeta_cutoffs(build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]]))
assert got == (3, 2), got

tests.name: finishing a loop normally is not a cutoff
tests.src:
# every value at this node makes the loop run to completion -- no child
# is ever skipped, so this node itself contributes 0 cutoffs
tree = build([5, 5, 5])
got = alphabeta_cutoffs(tree)
if got[1] != 0:
    raise AssertionError(
        "a node that examines every child without skipping any should "
        "not count as a cutoff, even though its call is about to return")

problems.title: One Function Instead of Two: Negamax
problems.blurb: max_value and min_value are mirror images of each other -- negate the value and swap the roles of alpha and beta, and one function does both jobs.
problems.statement:
Every alpha-beta implementation so far has needed two nearly-identical functions, max_value and min_value, that differ only by which comparison operator and which of alpha/ beta gets updated. Negamax is the standard trick real game engines use to collapse them into one: score every leaf from the mover's own point of view, and negate the value on the way back up.

Write negamax(node, alpha, beta, color), where color is 1 or -1: multiply a leaf's stored value by color before returning it, so a node always evaluates its own position as "good for me." Recurse with -beta, -alpha (the window flips and swaps) and -color (the next level scores from the other side), negate what comes back, and keep only the best (largest) result -- there is no separate "take the min" branch anymore, because negation already turned every level's job into "pick the biggest."

The single cutoff condition is value >= beta, checked after every child, exactly like MAX's condition in ordinary alpha-beta -- because negamax reframes every level as a maximizing one.
problems.examples:
>>> tree = build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]])
>>> negamax(tree, float('-inf'), float('inf'), 1)
3
>>> negamax(tree, float('-inf'), float('inf'), -1)
-6
hints: Base case: a leaf returns color * node.value -- flip the sign only at the leaves, where a real value first appears.
Recursive case: value = float('-inf'); for each child: v = -negamax(child, -beta, -alpha, -color); take value = max(value, v); alpha = max(alpha, value); then cut off if value >= beta.
Compare this shape to your ordinary max_value: negamax's loop is exactly max_value's loop, with min_value nowhere to be seen -- the negation is what makes a single function correct for every level.

tests.name: a lone leaf, both colors
tests.src:
assert negamax(build(7), float('-inf'), float('inf'), 1) == 7
assert negamax(build(7), float('-inf'), float('inf'), -1) == -7

tests.name: figure 5.2 from MAX's side matches ordinary alpha-beta
tests.src:
tree = build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]])
got = negamax(tree, float('-inf'), float('inf'), 1)
assert got == 3, got

tests.name: figure 5.2 from MIN's side is the negation of MAX's
tests.src:
tree = build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]])
got = negamax(tree, float('-inf'), float('inf'), -1)
assert got == -6, got

problems.title: Searching Depth 1, Then 2, Then 3
problems.blurb: A real engine doesn't pick a depth and hope -- it searches shallow first, deeper if there's time, keeping the best answer found so far at every step.
problems.statement:
Real game engines rarely search to one fixed depth. Time is limited and unpredictable, so instead they search depth 1, then depth 2, then depth 3, and so on -- keeping the best move found at each completed depth -- and stop whenever they run out of time. This is iterative deepening, and it means the engine always has a legal answer ready, even if it gets cut off mid-search.

Write iterative_deepening(node, max_limit): for every depth limit from 1 up to and including max_limit, run alpha-beta for MAX at the root at that depth, and collect the results. Return a list of (limit, move, value, leaves) tuples, one per depth, in increasing order of limit. As with any depth-limited search, every node needs a value ready in case the limit stops there, so the tree below carries a heuristic estimate at every level.

Each depth is searched independently and from scratch -- nothing carries over between them. That repeats a lot of work (everything depth 2 does, depth 3 does again and then some), which seems wasteful, but the shallow searches are cheap compared to the deepest one, and the guarantee of always having an answer ready is usually worth far more than the redundant computation costs.
hints: This calls for the exact alpha-beta-with-a-depth-limit function you've already built elsewhere -- max_value/min_value taking (subtree, alpha, beta, depth) and returning (value, move, leaves) -- run once per limit.

Loop limit from 1 to max_limit inclusive (range(1, max_limit + 1)). For each limit, call your depth-limited search fresh, with a brand new alpha=-inf, beta=inf window -- don't reuse state between limits.
Append (limit, move, value, leaves) to a results list each time, and return the whole list at the end.

tests.name: a single depth returns a one-element list
depths accumulate -- earlier results are not thrown away
tests.src:
tree = build((0, [(4, [(2, [7, 1]), (9, [3, 8])]), (6, [(5, [2, 6]), (1, [9, 9])]), (3, [(8, [4, 5])])]))
got = iterative_deepening(tree, 3)
assert len(got) == 3, got
assert [limit for limit, m, v, l in got] == [1, 2, 3], got

tests.name: the worked example: the chosen move itself changes with depth
each depth matches a fresh, independent call at that same limit

problems.title: Dominoes Against an Opponent Who Never Plans Ahead
problems.blurb: Same DominoesGame class, but the opponent always plays get_random_move -- so MIN's worst case is the wrong model, and CHANCE's average is the right one.
problems.statement:
Same board, same 1×2 pieces, same vertical/ horizontal roles as the homework. The one thing that changes: your opponent isn't out to beat you. Every turn, they call something exactly like the homework's own get_random_move -- they pick uniformly at random among their own legal moves, with no strategy at all.

Playing minimax against a player like that is needlessly cautious: it prepares for their worst possible move, when in reality every legal move is equally likely, including plenty of bad ones for them. Expectimax is the right tool whenever you know your opponent's policy isn't adversarial -- average over what they'll actually do, rather than assuming they'll do whatever hurts you most.

Write the class, method for method as in the homework, but with get_expectimax_move(vertical, limit) in place of get_best_move: your own turns are MAX nodes exactly as before, but the opponent's turns are CHANCE nodes, averaging uniformly over every legal move they could make. The evaluation itself is unchanged from the homework -- your legal moves minus theirs, always from the vertical passed to the call.
problems.examples:
>>> g = create_dominoes_vs_random_game(2, 2)
>>> g.get_expectimax_move(True, 1)
((0, 0), 1, 2)
>>> g = create_dominoes_vs_random_game(2, 3)
>>> move, value, leaves = g.get_expectimax_move(True, 2)
>>> move
(0, 1)
hints: Everything through successors() is identical to the homework's DominoesGame -- copy that structure over unchanged.

get_expectimax_move needs two helpers instead of max_value/min_value: max_value(game, vert_flag, depth) for your turns, chance_value(game, vert_flag, depth) for the opponent's. Both stop on depth == 0 or game_over(vert_flag), returning (evaluate(game), None, 1).

chance_value has no move to choose -- collect every successor into a list, recurse into max_value on each, sum the values, and divide by how many successors there were. If there's only one, that's fine -- dividing by 1 changes nothing.

There is no alpha, no beta, no cutoff anywhere in this search. Expectimax can't safely prune the way alpha-beta does, since a chance node's value depends on every child, not just the best or worst one -- skipping any of them changes the average.

tests.name: stores the board and creates empty boards of any shape
tests.src:
board = [[False, True], [False, False]]
assert DominoesVsRandomGame(board).get_board() is board
assert create_dominoes_vs_random_game(2, 3).get_board() == [[False]*3]*2

tests.src:

game = DominoesVsRandomGame([row[:] for row in board])
assert game.is_legal_move(0, 0, False) is False
assert game.is_legal_move(1, 0, False) is True
assert list(game.legal_moves(False)) == [(1, 0)]

tests.name: perform_move fills in place and returns None; game_over is player-specific
tests.src:
board = [[False] * 2 for _ in range(2)]
game = DominoesVsRandomGame(board)
assert game.perform_move(0, 0, True) is None
assert board == [[True, False], [True, False]]
assert game.game_over(True) is False, (
    "a vertical move still fits at (0, 1)")
assert game.game_over(False) is True, (
    "column 0 is fully blocked, and column 1 alone can't fit a "
    "horizontal piece")
assert DominoesVsRandomGame([[True, True], [True, True]]).game_over(True) is True

tests.name: copy is deep and successors leave the original untouched
tests.src:
original = DominoesVsRandomGame([[False] * 3 for _ in range(2)])
twin = original.copy()
assert isinstance(twin, DominoesVsRandomGame)
assert twin.get_board() == original.get_board()
assert all(a is not b for a, b in zip(twin.get_board(), original.get_board()))
pairs = list(original.successors(True))
assert original.get_board() == [[False] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
assert [m for m, _ in pairs] == [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2)]

tests.name: no alpha-beta pruning is happening: every leaf under the limit is touched
tests.src:
# on an empty board every move has an identical evaluation, so an
# expectimax search (which cannot prune) must still visit every one of
# them -- unlike alpha-beta, which could stop early on a tie
board = [[False] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
move, value, leaves = DominoesVsRandomGame(board).get_expectimax_move(True, 1)
assert leaves == 6, (
    "expectimax cannot prune -- every child must be visited to average "
    "over them, so leaves should equal the full branching factor")

tests.name: get_expectimax_move: minimax's worst-case model gives the wrong value here
tests.src:
board, vertical, limit, want, mistakes = ([[False, True, True, False], [False, False, False, False]], True, 2, ((0, 0), 0.5, 4), [('always_max', ((0, 0), 1, 4)), ('used_min', ((0, 0), 0, 4))])
got = DominoesVsRandomGame([row[:] for row in board]).get_expectimax_move(vertical, limit)
if got != want and got == dict(mistakes).get("used_min"):
    raise AssertionError(
        "%r: this looks like ordinary minimax (taking the opponent's "
        "worst move for you) instead of averaging over all of their "
        "legal moves -- the opponent here is random, not adversarial"
        % (got,))
assert got == want, (got, want)

problems.title: Triominoes Against the Same Careless Opponent
problems.blurb: 1x3 pieces this time, on top of the same MAX/CHANCE structure -- practice recognizing which parts of a variant carry over and which don't.
problems.statement:
Combine the two variations you've already seen separately: pieces are 1×3, like the homework-length gym's own triominoes problem, and the opponent plays uniformly at random, like DominoesVsRandomGame above. Nothing else changes.

Write the class the same way: is_legal_move needs the triominoes-style three-cell bounds check (reaching two squares past the anchor, not one), while get_expectimax_move(vertical, limit) needs the MAX/CHANCE structure from DominoesVsRandomGame, completely unchanged. Recognizing which parts of a variant transfer directly and which don't is the actual point of this problem.
problems.examples:
>>> g = create_triominoes_vs_random_game(3, 3)
>>> g.is_legal_move(0, 0, True), g.is_legal_move(1, 0, True)
(True, False)
>>> move, value, leaves = g.get_expectimax_move(True, 1)
>>> move
(0, 0)
hints: is_legal_move: build the three cells the piece would cover, then check each is in bounds and empty -- same shape as the gym I triominoes problem.
get_expectimax_move: identical structure to DominoesVsRandomGame's -- max_value for your turns, chance_value averaging over the opponent's, no alpha, no beta, no cutoff anywhere.
If you're tempted to add pruning here, stop -- expectimax can't safely skip any child of a chance node, since the average needs every one of them.

problems.title: Last Stone Wins, Against a Coin Flip
problems.blurb: The homework's take-away game against an opponent who picks their take uniformly at random -- the win/loss value becomes a genuine expectation, not just +-1.
problems.statement:
Same take-away game as the alpha-beta gym: a pile of stones, each player takes between 1 and max_take on their turn, and whoever takes the last stone wins. This time your opponent picks their take uniformly at random among their legal options, instead of playing to beat you.

Write get_expectimax_move(self, limit) on TakeAwayVsRandomGame (given, along with game_over, legal_moves, and successors), returning (move, value, leaves) for the player about to move -- structurally identical to the earlier TakeAwayGame's search, with chance_value in place of min_value.

The terminal scoring is unchanged: +1 if the pile is empty and it's the opponent's turn (you took the last stone), -1 if it's empty and it's your own turn, 0 at the depth horizon. What changes is what those numbers mean once CHANCE is averaging over them: the value get_expectimax_move returns is no longer just +1 or -1 -- it becomes a genuine expectation, a number between them representing how good this position is against a random opponent on average, not in the worst case.
hints: Same shape as TakeAwayGame's search: max_value(game, depth) for your turn, chance_value(game, depth) for the opponent's. Both stop on game.game_over() (returning the terminal +-1) or depth == 0 (returning 0), same as before.
chance_value has no move to track -- gather every successor into a list, recurse into max_value on each, average the results (sum divided by count), and return (average, None, total_leaves).
There's no alpha, no beta, no cutoff condition anywhere here -- expectimax needs every child's value to compute an average, so nothing can be safely skipped.

    "expectimax cannot prune -- every branch at every depth must be "
    "visited to average over it")

problems.title: Pig: Bank Your Points, or Push Your Luck
problems.blurb: A real six-sided die, not a metaphor for an opponent -- chance nodes here are actual random outcomes, with real 1-in-6 probabilities.
problems.statement:
Pig is a classic dice game: on your turn you repeatedly roll a die, adding each result to your turn total -- until you either choose to bank those points (locking them in and ending your turn), or roll a 1, which busts your whole turn total back to zero and ends it immediately regardless.

Write pig_decision(turn_score, limit): given your current (not-yet-banked) turn total, decide whether to "bank" or "roll", returning (action, expected_value, leaves), the same action-first convention every search in this gym returns. expected_value is how many points you can expect to walk away with from this point on, playing optimally, looking no more than limit further rolls ahead. Every one of the 6 die faces is a genuine CHANCE outcome with probability 1/6 -- this is the first problem in the gym where a chance node isn't a stand-in for an opponent, it's real randomness.

Two choices are available at every decision point:

  • "bank" is worth exactly turn_score -- guaranteed, no chance involved.
  • "roll" is a chance node over the 6 faces: rolling a 1 (probability 1/6) busts, worth 0; rolling 2 through 6 (each probability 1/6) adds that face to turn_score and hands you a brand new decision one ply deeper, worth whatever the best of banking-or-rolling then turns out to be.

Take the larger of the two. At the depth limit, assume you'd bank right now -- the same value banking would give regardless, so it doubles as a sensible cutoff heuristic with no extra work.
hints: Base case: limit == 0. Assume you bank right now -- return (turn_score, 'bank', 1).

bank_value is just turn_score. For roll_value, loop face in range(1, 7): face == 1 contributes 0 to the running total (and counts as 1 leaf on its own, since a bust needs no further recursion); face 2 through 6 recurses into pig_decision(turn_score + face, limit - 1), and you need its value (not its action) added into the total.

roll_value is that total divided by 6 -- all six faces are equally likely. Compare roll_value to bank_value and return whichever is larger, with 'roll' or 'bank' to match, and the leaves from every recursive call summed together (a bust face contributes exactly 1 leaf of its own).

tests.name: at the horizon, banking is the only option
tests.src:
assert pig_decision(0, 0) == ('bank', 0, 1)
assert pig_decision(15, 0) == ('bank', 15, 1)

tests.name: one roll ahead from zero: rolling beats banking nothing
tests.src:
got = pig_decision(0, 1)
assert got == ('roll', 10 / 3, 7), got

tests.name: with a big turn total already banked up, one more roll isn't worth the bust risk
tests.src:
# both options are still fully evaluated -- expectimax cannot know
# rolling is worse without exploring every one of its six outcomes
got = pig_decision(20, 1)
assert got == ('bank', 20, 7), got

tests.name: rolling always explores exactly 6 outcomes per level -- no pruning
tests.src:

assert leaves > 7, (
    "two levels of a 6-outcome chance node should visit well more than "
    "7 leaves -- expectimax cannot skip any outcome")

problems.title: L-Trominoes: Four Orientations, Not Two
problems.blurb: A piece with 4 rotations instead of 2 -- bounds-checking becomes 'does this 2x2 block fit', not 'does this row or column range fit'.
problems.statement:
Same rules as the homework -- two players alternate placing pieces on a Boolean grid, last player able to move wins -- with an L-shaped piece instead of a straight one. An L-tromino covers 3 of the 4 cells in some 2×2 block, in one of 4 orientations (which corner is left out):

0: X X     1: X X     2: X .     3: . X
    X .         . X         X X         X X

The "vertical" player may only use orientations 0 and 1; the "horizontal" player only 2 and 3 -- an arbitrary but fixed split, playing the same role the homework's vertical/horizontal distinction played, just applied to rotations instead of a straight line's direction.

Write the class: is_legal_move(row, col, orientation) checks that row, col anchors a 2×2 block fully on the board with all 3 of that orientation's cells empty. legal_moves(vertical) yields (row, col, orientation) in row-major order over (row, col), trying the smaller orientation number first at each cell. get_best_move(vertical, limit) is alpha-beta exactly as in the homework, scoring a board as the caller's legal moves minus the opponent's.
problems.examples:
>>> g = create_ltromino_game(3, 3)
>>> g.is_legal_move(0, 0, 0), g.is_legal_move(2, 2, 0)
(True, False)
>>> list(g.legal_moves(True))[:3]
[(0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), (0, 1, 0)]
>>> create_ltromino_game(3, 3).get_best_move(True, 1)
((1, 0, 1), 1, 8)
hints: cells(row, col, orientation) just looks up OFFSETS[orientation] and adds (row, col) to each pair. is_legal_move checks every cell that comes back is in bounds and empty -- the same structure as every earlier is_legal_move, just with 3 arbitrary offsets instead of a straight line.
orientations(vertical) returns (0, 1) if vertical else (2, 3). legal_moves loops row, then col, then each orientation in that tuple, checking is_legal_move each time.

Everything from perform_move through get_best_move is a direct copy of the homework's structure -- perform_move fills whatever cells() returns, and get_best_move's alpha-beta doesn't care at all how many orientations there are, only that successors() hands it (move, child) pairs.

problems.title: Dominoes on a Board With Holes in It
problems.blurb: A third cell state, permanently blocked -- occupancy checks need a real comparison now, not just a truthy/falsy test.
problems.statement:
Same rules as the homework, but the board isn't just True/False anymore. Each cell holds one of three states: EMPTY = 0, FILLED = 1 (a domino sits there), or BLOCKED = 2 (permanently unusable -- a hole in the board, never fillable by either player, present from the very start and never changing).

Write the class the same way as the homework, with one change threaded through everything that checks a cell: is_legal_move must check self.board[r][c] == EMPTY, not not self.board[r][c] -- a blocked cell is falsy-adjacent in neither direction, and treating BLOCKED as available (or treating it like FILLED some places and not others) breaks the search. perform_move sets a cell to FILLED, never to True. Everything else -- legal_moves, game_over, copy, successors, get_best_move -- is structurally identical to the homework.
problems.examples:
>>> g = BlockedDominoesGame([[0, 2], [0, 0]])
>>> g.is_legal_move(0, 0, True), g.is_legal_move(0, 0, False)
(True, False)
>>> g.perform_move(0, 0, True)
>>> g.get_board()
[[1, 2], [1, 0]]
>>> g.game_over(False)
True
hints: is_legal_move: same bounds check as the homework, then compare every relevant cell against EMPTY with == rather than checking truthiness -- self.board[row][col] == EMPTY and self.board[row+1][col] == EMPTY (or the horizontal pair).

perform_move sets cells to FILLED (the integer 1), not True. Since FILLED == 1 == True in Python, mixing them up won't crash -- but BLOCKED == 2 is truthy too, so any code that checks 'if self.board[r][c]:' instead of '== EMPTY' will wrongly treat a blocked cell the same as a filled one, which happens to give the right answer for occupancy but the wrong one anywhere you need to tell BLOCKED and FILLED apart.
get_best_move, successors, copy, game_over -- none of them look at individual cell values at all, only at is_legal_move's output, so they're identical to the homework's, untouched.

problems.title: Dominoes: Whoever Places More Pieces Wins
problems.blurb: A completely different win condition -- the game runs until nobody can move at all, and the piece count decides, not who moved last.
problems.statement:
Same board, same 1×2 pieces, same vertical/ horizontal roles -- a different objective entirely. The game continues until the board is jammed for both orientations at once (neither a vertical nor a horizontal move exists anywhere), which can easily happen with empty squares still on the board. Whoever has placed more total pieces by that point wins; equal counts are a draw.

This changes what game_over and the evaluation need to track. There's no single player who "runs out of moves" the way the homework's game_over(vertical) checked -- a vertical move being unavailable doesn't end anything if a horizontal one still is. is_jammed() (given, along with the rest of the game mechanics below) checks both orientations at once.

Write get_best_move(self, vertical, limit), given everything through perform_move and is_jammed. It needs to track piece counts alongside the board through the whole search -- each node needs to know how many pieces the caller has placed so far along this line of play, and how many the opponent has, not just what the board looks like. At a jammed position, score +1 if the caller placed more pieces than the opponent, -1 if fewer, 0 if tied. At the depth horizon with the game still going, score 0 -- there's no cheap heuristic here the way "my moves minus theirs" was in the homework, since what matters is a running count, not the current board shape.

One rule the homework never needed, because it couldn't arise there: a player can be stuck in their own orientation while the game keeps going. If it's your turn and no vertical move exists anywhere, but a horizontal move still does somewhere, the board is not jammed -- your opponent can still move. You simply pass: no piece placed, no count incremented, and it becomes the other player's turn, still consuming one level of the search. Only when neither orientation has a move anywhere does the game actually end. A plain empty board can reach this the very first time either side runs low on room, so this isn't a rare edge case to special-case away -- it needs to be part of the ordinary recursive step.
hints: You need to carry (board, my_pieces, opp_pieces) as one bundle through the whole recursion -- not just a board. The simplest way is to pass my_pieces and opp_pieces as extra parameters alongside game/depth in both helpers, incrementing the right one by 1 every time perform_move is actually called.

Base case: if game.is_jammed(): compare my_pieces to opp_pieces directly (1 if greater, -1 if less, 0 if equal) -- not evaluate() on the board, since the board alone can't tell you who placed more pieces to reach it. If depth == 0 and the game isn't jammed, return 0 -- there's nothing else safe to guess.

Before looping: collect this player's legal_moves(vert_flag) into a list. If it's empty but is_jammed() was already False, this player must pass -- recurse straight into the other helper with the same board and the same piece counts, depth - 1, and return whatever that call returns (with move = None). Only build the ordinary max/min loop when there's at least one real move.

Structure is otherwise ordinary alpha-beta: max_value(game, vert_flag, my_pieces, opp_pieces, alpha, beta, depth) recurses into min_value with my_pieces + 1 (you just placed a piece) and opp_pieces unchanged; min_value recurses into max_value with opp_pieces + 1 and my_pieces unchanged. Everything else -- the alpha/beta updates, the cutoff checks, the leaf count -- is identical to the homework's.

assert got == want, (got, want)

problems.title: Triominoes, With Nobody Owning an Orientation Either
problems.blurb: 1x3 pieces plus no fixed roles at once -- the two variant dimensions from earlier problems, stacked on top of each other.
problems.statement:
Combine both twists you've already worked through separately: pieces are 1×3, and nobody is locked into vertical or horizontal -- anyone may place either way on their turn, every turn.

Nothing about either half of this is new. The bounds-and-empty check needs the triominoes' three-cell reach; the evaluation needs the free-orientation problem's insight that "my moves minus theirs" is useless when both players share one legal_moves(), so get_best_move(limit) needs the same win/loss-at-the-horizon scoring as before -- -1 for a MAX node with no moves, +1 for a MIN node with none, 0 at the depth limit. The only real work here is recognizing that the two variations don't interact at all: each piece of the class only cares about one of them.
problems.examples:
>>> g = create_free_triominoes_game(3, 3)
>>> sorted(g.legal_moves())[:2]
[(0, 0, False), (0, 0, True)]
>>> create_free_triominoes_game(3, 3).get_best_move(1)
((0, 0, True), 0, 6)
hints: is_legal_move and cells(): copy directly from the triominoes-game problem -- this half of the class hasn't changed at all.
legal_moves() and game_over(): copy directly from free-dominoes-game, just yielding a third element (the orientation) since there's no longer a single fixed orientation per call.

get_best_move(limit): identical structure to free-dominoes-game's -- no vertical parameter anywhere, terminal values are still +-1 by which side has no move, depth == 0 with the game still going is still 0.

board = [[False, True], [False, False]]

CASES = [([[False, False, False], [False, False, False], [False, False, False]], [(0, 0, True), (0, 0, False), (0, 1, True), (0, 2, True), (1, 0, False), (2, 0, False)]), ([[False, False, False, False], [False, False, False, False], [False, False, False, False]], [(0, 0, True), (0, 0, False), (0, 1, True), (0, 1, False), (0, 2, True), (0, 3, True), (1, 0, False), (1, 1, False), (2, 0, False), (2, 1, False)])]
for board, want in CASES:
    got = list(FreeTriominoesGame([r[:] for r in board]).legal_moves())

board = [[False] * 4 for _ in range(3)]
game = FreeTriominoesGame(board)
assert game.perform_move(0, 0, False) is None

tests.name: copy is independent and successors never touch the original
tests.src:
original = FreeTriominoesGame([[False] * 4 for _ in range(3)])
twin = original.copy()
assert all(a is not b for a, b in zip(twin.get_board(), original.get_board()))
list(original.successors())
assert original.get_board() == [[False] * 4 for _ in range(3)]

tests.name: get_best_move: the homework's per-orientation formula doesn't apply here either
tests.src:
board, limit, want, mistakes = ([[False, False, False], [False, False, False], [False, False, False]], 3, ((0, 0, True), 1, 7), [('flat_formula', ((0, 0, True), 0, 7)), ('always_neg', ((0, 0, True), -1, 7)), ('no_window', ((0, 0, True), 1, 12)), ('strict_cut', ((0, 0, True), 1, 12)), ('ties_last', ((2, 0, False), 1, 7))])
got = FreeTriominoesGame([r[:] for r in board]).get_best_move(limit)
if got != want and got == dict(mistakes).get("flat_formula"):
    raise AssertionError(
        "%r: both players share legal_moves() here -- a move-count "
        "difference is always 0. Score wins and losses at the horizon "
        "instead." % (got,))
assert got == want, (got, want)
